text:
Early July sits in Sólmánuður, the month of the sun, when the light barely leaves and the nights hold a pale grey rather than dark. The grass has come up thick, the lambs have put on weight, and the hay is standing ready to be cut — this is the part of the Icelandic year when what was sown has become something countable. Fehu belongs to that stretch honestly, because it is the rune of what has grown enough to be measured.

Fehu means cattle. In the old northern world, a household's wealth was its livestock, so the same word did the work of both, and the rune carries the two meanings without separating them. Its shape is two strokes angled upward from an upright line, read by many as the horns of an animal, though the shape matters less than what the name holds. Wealth, in this rune, is not coin alone — it is anything that can be held, counted, lost, or handed on. Cattle is that same wealth in its living form, the kind that eats and breeds and must be tended through winter or it dies. Material prosperity is the condition of having enough of it, the state where the byre is full and the household is provided for. These three belong together because they were once one thing: a herd was the goods, the goods were alive, and the prosperity was only as sound as the care given to the animals. So Fehu is wealth understood as something that moves — it comes in, it must be fed, and it goes out again, whether as trade, as gift, or as loss. Its other side appears when the holding becomes the whole point, when what is owned is hoarded past use or counted past reason, and also when the herd is thin and the winter is long; the rune names lack as readily as plenty, since both are conditions of the same wealth. It promises nothing about how much anyone will have, Kuky, nor that what is gained will stay. Fehu is the rune of what can be owned, and of the fact that owning is a kind of work.

Early July falls in Sólmánuður, the month of the sun — the stretch when the light never fully leaves, the grass stands thick enough to cut, and the lambs on the hillsides have put on real weight. This is the fattest part of the Icelandic year, the weeks when what the land will give has mostly been given and the counting can begin. Fehu belongs here plainly, because this is the season of increase made visible.

Fehu means cattle. The word behind it is the old word for livestock, the same root that gives us fee and fief — payment, holding, what a person owns. Its shape, two arms angled upward from a single upright, is often read as the horns of an animal, and that reading sits well with the name. In the world the rune comes from, cattle were not a symbol of wealth; they were wealth itself, the thing you counted to know what you had. So the rune holds wealth in the most ordinary sense — grain in the store, animals in the field, coin in the hand. It holds prosperity as well, which is wealth over time rather than wealth in a moment: the herd that keeps calving, the land that keeps yielding. And it holds the material world without apology, the fact that bodies need feeding and roofs need mending. These meanings are one rune because they are one thing seen at different distances — the animal, the herd, the years of herds. Turned too far, Fehu becomes hoarding, the counting that never stops and never satisfies, wealth held so tightly it does no work; absent, it is the empty byre and the thin winter, want with nothing to draw on. It promises no sum, no gain, no security, Kuky, and it says nothing about what wealth is spent on or whether it is deserved. Fehu is the rune of what can be owned, and of the truth that what is owned must be kept moving or it rots.

Sólmánuður, the month of the midnight sun, holds the early days of July in the Icelandic year — the grass stands high, the lambs are fattening on the heath, and the light does not leave the sky. This is the stretch when the land gives most freely, when a farm can see what it will have by autumn and count it. Fehu sits well in such a time, because it is the rune of what can be counted.

Fehu is the first rune of the older row, and its name means cattle — livestock, the animals a household kept. In an old farming world, cattle were wealth itself: they were food, they were trade, they were what a family owned and what it could lose in a hard winter. The shape of the rune is a single upright stave with two short arms angled upward from one side, often read as the horns of an animal, or as a hand held open to take and to give. Wealth, in this rune, means portable goods — not land, not birthright, but the kind of holding that moves, multiplies, and can be handed to another. Material prosperity is the fuller state of that: enough in the store, enough to feed the household and still have something over. Cattle bind the two together, because a cow is at once a possession and a thing that breeds more possessions — wealth that eats, grows, and must be tended daily or it dwindles. So the rune's meanings are not three ideas but one, seen at three distances: the animal, the goods, the sufficiency.

Its other side is plain enough. Wealth that is only hoarded turns to weight, and wealth that is only spent leaves nothing standing by spring; a herd too large for the pasture starves as surely as a herd too small to feed anyone. When Fehu is absent, the matter is want — not poverty as a moral state, but the simple lack of what is needed, and the narrowing that comes with it. The rune promises no fortune to Kuky and no ruin either. It names a thing that moves and must keep moving to stay alive.
